title: The letters as letters
hookLine: Paul's letters are real post: greetings, travel plans, and a list of friends' names (Romans 16)

cards: When did a real letter last land in your mailbox? Paper, not email: maybe a card from a grandparent, with the news, a little advice, and a list at the end: say hi to your mom, love to the kids.
A whole run of New Testament books carry Paul's name, and they aren't essays or sermons. They're letters. Real mail, sent to real people in real cities: Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica.
Somebody carried them by hand, over roads and seas, and somebody read them aloud to a room full of people who knew the sender. At the very end of Romans is a page that's easy to skip.

teach.b: Today's word is epistle, from the Greek for something sent.

Paul's letters follow the usual letter shape of his day: who it's from, who it's to, a greeting, grace and peace, then thanks, the business, travel plans, and hellos. Romans chapter sixteen is almost all hellos.

It opens, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." A note printed after Romans in the King James says the letter was sent by her.
Then come more than twenty-five names. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a married couple who risked their necks for him, with a church meeting in their house.
Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with him. Tryphena and Tryphosa, who work hard. Rufus, and his mother, who was a mother to Paul too.
Some he calls his kinsmen, fellow Jews; others have Greek and Latin names. Women and men, side by side.
Near the end, a different voice breaks in: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Tertius is the scribe, writing as Paul speaks, adding his own hello.
In other letters Paul takes the pen at the end and signs in his own big handwriting. In one he asks a friend to bring the coat he left behind, and his books.
Why does it matter? The letters now read in church as scripture started as mail between friends. Christians read them as God's word, and they never stopped being letters, full of names.

how: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches, a reading from one of the New Testament letters, often called the Epistle, is read aloud at Sunday worship, the way the letters were first heard by the churches they were sent to.

s: Paul's letters were written as essays for the whole world
they're real mail to real churches, with greetings, travel plans and names.
Romans 16 names more than twenty-five people
women and men, Jewish, Greek and Latin names, side by side.
Paul wrote every word of his letters by hand
he used a scribe for Romans. Tertius adds his own greeting in Romans 16, and Paul signs some letters himself.

games.q: you're Tertius. you've just written down Paul's whole long letter to Rome, word for word. there's room at the end. what do you do?
o: add your own greeting to the church.
games.why: he adds his own line: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord. the scribe is remembered by name.

practice: Begin one real letter or card in your head, to someone who'd be surprised to hear from you.

Start the way Paul did, with a greeting, then one specific thing you're grateful for about them, some ordinary news, and a list of names to say hello to. If you pray, you can pray for each name as it comes.

orig.note: Greek: a letter, something sent, from epistello, to send to. Latin epistola gave us epistle.
